extracted.intended_audience: journalism researchers, communication scholars, journalism educators, and interested journalists
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and descriptive standards for producing and evaluating journalistic newswriting, focusing on the role of discourse knowledge (genre conventions) versus audience knowledge during the newswriting process. Draws on protocol-analysis observations of science journalists to illustrate each criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discourse knowledge (genre conventions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Information about the standards and conventions of a particular genre of writing — 'an array of rhetorical choices about appropriate formats, matters of tone, diction, stance toward the reader, kinds of allowable openings, structure, evidence, and argument' (Park, 1986). Discourse knowledge is often tacit but can surface in working memory to guide composing decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers retrieve discourse knowledge from long-term memory into working memory to make decisions; it governs choices of format, tone, diction, openings, structure, evidence and argument. Use images of prior texts as heuristics (Flower, 1987). Discourse knowledge tends to guide moment-to-moment decisions more than explicit audience modeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discourse community / acquisition of conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers obtain discourse knowledge from a specific 'discourse community' — a group bound by common interest that communicates through approved channels and regulates discourse (Porter, 1986).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn conventions by reading texts published in approved forums (topics, organizational structures, styles), by socialization (education, professional experience), handing texts to colleagues, revising guided by editors, and modeling the 'public idiom.' Prior published texts function as heuristics guiding composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience knowledge (reader-centered awareness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Information about audience members' knowledge, needs, interests, experiences, beliefs, attitudes and expectations — the standard admonition to 'write for readers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although widely advised, the study finds journalists rarely recall or use audience knowledge during newswriting. The paper notes assessing a mass audience is difficult because it is heterogeneous; audience knowledge may be invoked occasionally (e.g., 'readers may want to know') but is not the primary driver of moment-to-moment drafting decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: News values
rubrics_metrics.description: The news values held by journalists and editors (e.g., prominence, timeliness, proximity, rarity and consequence) that provide the cognitive basis for decisions about selection, attention, understanding and representation of news (van Dijk, 1988).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News values influence story selection and attention; in this study news values had less direct impact during the actual newswriting process (they may operate more strongly during newsgathering/idea selection). Examples: timeliness motivated choosing a Gulf War gas mask piece; prominence and consequence cited as selection criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear writing achieved through precise word choice, concise and direct sentence structure, grammatically-correct sentences, logical progression of thought from paragraph to paragraph, logical text organization, and sufficient background information and explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists actively monitor and revise for clarity during drafting: replace imprecise words ('Not rather, but more likely'), remove redundancy ('Get rid of some of this repetitive stuff'), reorganize material (move discovery into second paragraph), and adjust sentence phrasing ('That still doesn't sound quite right'). Clarity concerns drive frequent micro-revisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vividness
rubrics_metrics.description: Creating images or pictures and appealing to the senses through rich description, colorful language and literary techniques to make copy 'grabby' or 'punchier.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers balance vividness against other constraints (e.g., credibility). Examples: choosing a grabby lead, inserting imagery; explicit tradeoffs reported (dropping a title to 'make it a bit punchier' at cost of credibility). Vividness is assessed and adjusted during drafting, sometimes prioritized by individual journalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility (accuracy, sourcing, impartiality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Credible writing is accurate, factual and impartial; credibility is maintained through accurate facts, correct attributions, use of quotations, and selection of authoritative sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists frequently retrieve discourse knowledge about how and when to use direct quotes to 'achieve distance' and to support claims. They check exact wording of quotes, verify spellings, titles and facts, consult reference sources, evaluate source expertise (e.g., CDC, medical centers), and consider placement of quotations in the story ('Here is about the time in the story when I need to bring in a quote'). Credibility considerations often have the greatest impact on decision making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production constraints (space and time)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical constraints of the production environment — limited space (copy length) and time (deadlines) — that affect writing choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists 'write to space' and monitor word/line counts and time while composing ('Word count 386 words... I should probably write about 1,000'; 'I'm at line 46'). Space constraints determine when to stop adding material; time pressure can shorten revision or sourcing practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventional register / public idiom / mode of address
rubrics_metrics.description: The newsroom's conventional register — an accepted, imposed or expected way of writing — and the newspaper's 'version of the language of the public' that forms the mode of address to assumed readership (Hall et al., 1978; Andersen, 1987).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists learn the mode of address by modeling the publication's public idiom; the conventional register shapes diction, tone, and rhetorical choices more than individualized audience profiling. Teaching to 'think of the audience' may be less effective than teaching the conventional register and what 'works' in the discourse community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization and structural choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions about paragraphing, order of information (e.g., lead placement, moving discovery to second paragraph), use of examples, and overall logical set-up to enable later explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists make moment-to-moment structural decisions to preserve clarity and flow: start new paragraphs, group related paragraphs, move examples or discoveries earlier or later to support exposition, and restructure to provide space for later explanation. Structural heuristics are often drawn from prior texts and learned conventions.
